title: With game postponed, Oklahoma spends Saturday taking shots at Ole Miss, Paul Finebaum and SEC
content:
Oklahoma and Ole Miss aren’t playing until Sunday. That freed up Saturday to be all about arguing over the SEC’s decision to postpone their game.

Oklahoma athletic director Roger Denny went on a media tour, doubling and tripling down on his angry late-night statement about the game being moved to Sunday. Ole Miss spoke only through a statement in defense of why, after the FAA’s nationwide ground stop Friday, it was the only FBS team unable to travel to play Saturday.

The SEC office, which ultimately made the decision, declined comment. But Paul Finebaum, the SEC Network host and “carnival barker,” as Denny called him, shot back that the first-year athletic director was “pathetically pandering to his fan base.”

The whole situation has left ill feelings between Oklahoma, now in its third year in the SEC, and a conference that likes to handle things internally.

In an interview with SoonerScoop on Saturday, Denny was asked if the ordeal had hurt Oklahoma’s relationship with the conference. His response: “I don’t know.”

“They’ll probably send their carnival barker (Finebaum) out there to accuse me of pandering again, and candidly, I don’t care,” Denny told SoonerScoop. “My job and my duty is to our players, our university and to our fanbase. If they don’t like the way we handle our business, I just don’t much care about that.”

Finebaum had already teed up Denny by then, criticizing his late-night statement that called the postponement the wrong decision.

“What he did here is really against the code of the SEC to call out a commissioner during a national crisis and emergency,” Finebaum said on ESPN. “He’s thinking about himself and his fanbase, who’s already on tenterhooks because of the season, and I think he is dead wrong and quite frankly, I think it’s unbecoming of a leader in college athletics or anywhere to do what he did.”

In the end, Ole Miss and Oklahoma will play 1 p.m. ET Sunday in Norman, Okla., where the forecast calls for cold and rain. The Sooners are offering reduced concession prices and free hand warmers to fans.

SEC commissioner Greg Sankey had the discretion to reschedule the game, based on rule changes the conference made after a dispute between Florida and LSU when a hurricane affected their game in 2016. After Friday’s ground stop, the SEC spent the evening consulting with the four teams (Ole Miss, Tennessee, Texas and Auburn) that had not already flown to this weekend’s road games.

Auburn, which was playing at Mississippi State, quickly elected to go by bus. Texas and Tennessee secured new air charter times after the ground stop was lifted.

That left Ole Miss. The airport in Oxford is too small for big planes, so the Rebels typically fly out of Tupelo, about an hour’s drive away.

“The goal was always to fly to Norman Friday night and play the game Saturday,” Ole Miss said in a statement. “After the stoppage was lifted at 7:30 p.m., we began preparing the team for departure before our charter broker, Air Planning, informed us that JetBlue could not fly us Friday night. At that hour, due to the time required to rescreen the party and travel to the Tupelo airport, the crew’s duty time would have expired prior to departure. There were no other flight options at that point, and we determined it was too late to put our student-athletes on a bus trip of eight or more hours.”

The flight crew’s rest restrictions also meant Ole Miss could not fly out until Saturday afternoon “at the earliest.”

Ole Miss’ statement did not say whether Memphis, about 80 minutes north of Oxford with a bigger airport hub, was explored.

“We understand other SEC teams were able to keep their games on Saturday, with those visiting teams having available Friday charters or ability to bus to their game in four hours. We did not have those advantages,” Ole Miss’ statement read. “We regret that the game had to be moved to Sunday, but we took every reasonable action in our power to avoid this scenario. The ground stoppage has been an unfortunate ordeal for all of us, and we are grateful that a solution was reached to play our game.”

Denny was not grateful. His statement immediately after the decision was strong, and his comments Saturday afternoon were even stronger.

In his sit-down with SoonerScoop, Denny insinuated that Ole Miss (6-3, and still in CFP contention) angled for the postponement: “As early as 9 o’clock last night, we’re hearing from state highway patrol and local PD that Ole Miss is telling them the game’s going to be on Sunday, we’re not going to get here until late Saturday afternoon. The fact that that decision had been made by them by 9 o’clock, I think, speaks to just how many levers they were trying to pull to actually get here. The fact that we heard that from our highway patrol and not directly from the league office at that time is infuriating.”

Denny also suggested Ole Miss did not care as much about having one day less to prepare for its next opponent, Wofford, while Oklahoma plays Texas A&M next Saturday.

“If you’re the Ole Miss football team, do you want to come play at the palace on a Saturday night against a team and a fan base that’s got a lot of momentum and juice, or if the league’s going to give you the opportunity to push that game to a Sunday morning in the rain, you probably make that decision,” Denny said.

“The problem is the league office can’t let people force that issue. For too long, we’ve allowed institutions to make decisions and create circumstances that are in their individual best interest but unequivocally against the broader interest of college football and our peers in the conference, and the leaders of our industry haven’t stepped in. And this is yet another example of that.”
